name: Portal
technique: Spoofed sysvar account bypassed signature verification
classificationNote: Curated: reclassified from "signature-crypto" based on the published post-mortem.
rootCause: Wormhole's Solana program used the deprecated load_instruction_at, which did not verify that the passed "instructions sysvar" account was the real one. The attacker passed a fake sysvar, so guardian signature verification was skipped, and minted 120k wETH on Solana with no backing.

The attacker passed a fake sysvar, so guardian signature verification was skipped, and minted 120k wETH on Solana with no backing.
Wormhole had a loophole... A hacker distorted the fabric of Solana's space-time, netting $326M in the process. How did Wormhole return so much ETH so fast?

Attackers exploited a signature verification vulnerability in the Wormhole network to mint 120k Ether on Solana, worth over $326 million. The hack was made possible by a series of signature verification authorizations, where the developers used a deprecated function to enable unverified forged signature passes.

On February 2,3, 2022, an attacker exploited a signature-verification bug in the Wormhole Solana-side bridge contract, allowing unauthorized minting of 120,000 wETH (~$325M). Most of the unbacked assets were bridged to Ethereum and sold. Jump Crypto replenished the missing ETH, restoring Wormhole's 1:1 asset backing and containing broader systemic risk. The Solana-side Wormhole contract used a deprecated sysvar API for signature verification that failed to validate the instructions sysvar account provenance. The attacker supplied a forged account, bypassed guardian consensus, and minted wETH without ETH collateral. The fix was committed but not yet deployed.

Portal (Wormhole bridge) was exploited on Solana on February 2, 2022, through a Solana-side signature verification flaw that allowed the attacker to mint 120,000 unbacked wETH (~$325M). Jump Crypto replenished the loss, preserving asset backing. The Wormhole Solana contract failed to properly validate the canonical Instructions sysvar account during signature verification. This allowed attacker-controlled serialized instruction data to be accepted as guardian-signed verification, enabling unauthorized minting.
